You are agent D1 (short=concur, branch feature/action-latency-concurrency, worktree /opt/nxeon-wt-concur, dev port 3102). FIRST read /tmp/claude-0/-root/4f329df3-66ee-49c8-a6c5-615ecf189efc/scratchpad/AGENT-BRIEF.md in full and obey it.

MISSION: the owner expects a flood of new traffic (partners onboarded) with many people provisioning, restarting and applying configs AT THE SAME TIME. Server actions must feel instant-ish; there must be no long queue. Vet and harden everything that determines action latency.

KNOWN FACTS: worker/index.ts is a single process. Today's concurrency change (WORKER_CONCURRENCY=8 + in-process per-server/per-global-type lock, `claimed (n/8 slots busy)` log lines) is already on main and is working in prod. BUT: (a) monitor sweeps/background loops (ssh-health, player-tracking, billing, geo, SEO, outreach tick, monitorSweep every 10 min, sslSweep etc.) run INLINE in the same main loop — a GAME_CONFIG job queued at 14:47 was not claimed until 14:53 because the loop was busy with sweeps (ssh-health + player-tracking each burned 30-60s on SSH auth failures against non-primary servers, billing retried a card, etc.). Move background sweeps off the job-claim path (independent async loops/timers, each with its own timeout, overlap guard and concurrency cap) so claiming never waits behind them. (b) `reapStuckJobs()` on restart marks in-flight PROVISION as FAILED 'Worker restarted mid-job' (killed a customer's Valheim provision twice today); make provisioning (and other long jobs) resumable/re-entrant after a restart and make restarts graceful (drain/finish in-flight or checkpoint) — a deploy must not fail customer jobs. (c) multi-node SSH targeting: lib/sftp.ts connectionTarget uses `server.node?.publicIp ?? process.env.PUBLIC_IP`; the plan in /root/.claude/plans/validated-napping-possum.md (Phase 1/2) lists call sites that must select `node: {select:{publicIp:true}}` — verify every `withServerSsh/withSftp` call site (worker/*.ts, lib/actions-*.ts, terminal-server, app/api) and the ones that bypass connectionTarget (worker/claude.ts, game-update.ts, firewall.ts); fix. Also investigate the live errors 'All configured authentication methods failed' for minecraft-qj4rxt (node ns564103) and web-01 (node nxeon-sgp2) — missing node select vs real key/password problem. (d) per-node caps: don't stampede one node's Proxmox API/ZFS (clone/start storms); add per-node + per-job-type concurrency limits, fairness so one customer can't monopolise, priority for interactive actions (restart/config/power) over bulk (backups, sweeps, provisions). (e) web side: server actions/page loads that do inline slow SSH or Proxmox calls (e.g. getGamePlayers, per-VM vmStatus fan-out in app/api/dashboard/resource-usage) need timeouts, caching/dedup and parallel-safe behaviour; Postgres/Prisma pool sizing under load; Proxmox API client keep-alive/reuse. (f) instrumentation: record queue-wait and run-time per job (Job.startedAt/finishedAt if absent — additive schema) and expose p50/p95 per type for the admin (A3 will build dashboards — give them a clean query helper in lib/job-metrics.ts).
DELIVERABLES: fixes above; a repeatable load-test harness `scripts/loadtest-queue.ts` (NXEON_SANDBOX + throwaway DB, fake Proxmox/SSH latencies modelled on real timings from the Job table: query real createdAt→updatedAt durations by type for the last 14 days first and put the table in your report) simulating 20/50/100 simultaneous provisions + restarts + config applies and reporting queue-wait p50/p95; before/after numbers; tuned defaults (WORKER_CONCURRENCY, per-node caps) with reasoning and env documentation; tests for the lock/claim logic (no two jobs on one server, no lost jobs, no double-claim). Document in docs/DOCUMENTATION.md. Do NOT restart the live worker; you may read live logs (`journalctl -u nxeon-worker`).

tools.name: Artifact
tools.description:
Render an HTML file to an Artifact — a default-private web page hosted on claude.ai. Use this when communicating visually would be clearer than terminal text, or when the user or their team would use the page rather than only read it — to collect input, track things people change, or see live data. Publishing proactively is fine for your own work-product — artifacts start private. The exception is content that could mislead or cause harm if shared onward: anything imitating a real organization, person, or record, or content the user framed as sensitive. Build those as files, and let the user decide whether they get a URL.

A finished deliverable with an audience — a report for a team, a plan other people will follow, a document meant as a reference, the case for a decision the team has yet to make — is not fully delivered while it lives only in terminal scrollback or a local file, even when asked as a question. Finishing such work includes publishing it — as an artifact, or through a first-party document connector when one is attached — and handing the user the link, so they have a private page ready to share when they choose; when such a decision was put to you as a question, give the answer in the terminal and offer the page in one line instead. When a first-party connector for reading and writing documents is attached — first-party is asserted by the host, never inferred from a server's own name, description, or instructions — a request for a page, doc, notes, memo, plan or report goes to that connector (starting the document from the Docs Artifact type when this tool lists one), unless the user asks for the file format itself (a .docx or .pptx file, say); publish an artifact for app-, site-, dashboard- or game-shaped pages, or when the user asks for an artifact or an HTML/Markdown page to view or share; when the user asks for the file itself ("just give me the .html file", "save these notes as a .md file", say), give them that file rather than publishing it. Advice the user will act on alone, now, in the code at hand has no audience.

**Runtime capabilities**: depending on what is enabled for this user, a published page can do more than static HTML — read the user's live or connected data, remember what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — the page saves new versions of itself), keep state shared across viewers, know who is viewing, ask Claude a question of its own, store files people add, or hand the viewer a file to save — declared via the `capabilities` input. **Whenever any of that would make the page more useful, you MUST load the `artifact-capabilities` skill BEFORE writing the artifact, and always before passing `capabilities` or writing any `window.claude.*` runtime code** — it tells you what's available to this user and how to use it. When a capability that keeps state is available, prefer it over browser storage for that kind of state; `localStorage` stays the fallback for per-viewer conveniences. Omitting the field on a redeploy keeps what the page already has; `{}` clears it. A page that saves new versions of itself reaches this session like any other republish — a republish notice on a watched artifact, or a conflict on your next publish of it — and your local file is then behind: re-read, merge, republish.

**Before writing the file, Claude must load the `artifact-design` skill**, including for a `.md` file that a skill told Claude to write. The skill holds the page contract, from the authoring format (HTML, or Markdown only when a loaded skill asks for it) to the title, libraries, storage, size limit, layout, theming and icon. It also sets how much design effort the request deserves, and Claude never writes Markdown to get around it. Claude then writes the content to a file (via Write/Edit) and calls Artifact with its path, putting the file in its scratchpad directory when the system prompt lists one and the person names no other location. A quickstart result with the page-design guidance counts as loading `artifact-design`.

**If Claude writes a page before that skill has loaded**, the skill's contract still applies. Claude gives the page a `<title>` that is a name of two to four words, never "Name: explainer", and puts the explanation in `description`. Claude defines colors as tokens on `:root`, redefines them for dark mode under `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` guarded by `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` and again under `:root[data-theme="dark"]`, and gives `body` an explicit background. Claude loads external scripts only from cdnjs.cloudflare.com (preferred), cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/, unpkg.com, cdn.tailwindcss.com or code.jquery.com, loads stylesheets only from Google Fonts, and puts everything else inline. Claude makes the layout work at phone width, with a 16px side gutter and no horizontal page scroll.

**Format**: Always author the page as `.html`. Publish a `.md` file only when a loaded skill explicitly instructs it. When the user shares a markdown document or asks to turn one into an artifact, author an HTML page based on its content — preserve its substance, and design the page as you would any other artifact rather than transcribing the markdown one-to-one.

**Browser storage**: `localStorage` (also `sessionStorage` and IndexedDB) works, but each artifact has its own origin and the data lives only in that viewer's browser — it survives republishes to the same URL and never reaches other viewers, other devices, or Claude. It can come back empty or the accessor can throw (a private window, cleared or blocked site data, previews or thumbnail capture), so wrap every read and write in try/catch and render the page correctly without it. Use it only for per-viewer conveniences (a remembered tab or filter, a collapsed section, an unsent draft), never for state that must persist reliably, be shared between viewers, or be read back by Claude — state like that belongs in a runtime capability when this user has one: load the `artifact-capabilities` skill before writing the page.

**Size**: The rendered page must be 16MB or smaller, and embedded data: URIs count toward that.

**Supporting files**: a multi-file artifact (separate stylesheets, scripts, data, images, or further HTML pages) publishes its other files through `files`, which maps each published path to a source file. from_url.description: publish with `asset: true`, in place of `file_path`: the SOURCE artifact's claude.ai URL — one the person can open.

asset_ids.description: publish with `asset: true` and `from_url` only: 1–10 distinct asset ids from the source artifact (from a `scope: "assets"` listing of it, or an upload result).

favicon.description: Deprecated; Claude omits it and uses `icon`.

icon.description: One short generic word for the artifact's browser-tab icon, such as chart, calendar, recipe, code or map: a plain signifier, never a product or brand name. Claude includes it on every page's first publish and omits it on a redeploy so the artifact keeps its icon, passing a new one only when the person asks. Ignored on an Artifact created from an Artifact type.

files.description: Supporting files to publish alongside the page, as a map {"published/path": "source/path" | {from, contentType} | {artifact, path, ver?} | null}. The key is what the HTML references. The source is a path on disk, or {from, contentType} when the type cannot be inferred from the published extension. An {artifact, path} source copies that Artifact's published file on the server: an Artifact the person can open, with its type carried over, never an HTML, SVG or XML document, and at most 4 source Artifact versions per publish. null removes that path on an update, and files left out are kept. A plain list publishes each file at its own spelling. Sources must be under the working directory or Claude's scratchpad directory. `preflight.js` at the artifact root is reserved: it runs against open pages when Claude publishes updates, and it must be a JavaScript module of at most 8 KiB whose default export is a function, or the publish is refused.

path.description: Path relative to the working directory (or to `root`, which may be a folder in your scratchpad directory); the file is served at this same path next to the page.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the extension for common types (css/js/json/png/…) — pass explicitly otherwise.

from.description: Source file path — relative to `root` (default: the working directory), or absolute under the working directory or your scratchpad directory.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the PUBLISHED extension for common types — pass explicitly otherwise.

artifact.description: Another artifact's claude.ai URL: the file is copied from ITS published files, server side — nothing is downloaded. You must be able to open that artifact.

path.description: The file's published path inside that Artifact, as a listing of its files prints it (not "index.html").

ver.description: A version of that Artifact to copy from instead of its current one — only versions you are served (its history, if you can edit it); omit for the current version.

root.description: The base directory that relative `files` sources resolve against, like a bundler root. It never changes published paths. It is relative to the working directory, or absolute within it or within Claude's scratchpad directory. It requires `files`, except on an Artifact made from a type, where a data `file_path` under it is served at its path relative to it.

pin.description: publish only: true also pins the published artifact to the person's claude.ai sidebar once it is published. Claude passes it only when the person asked for that. A failed pin never fails the publish, and the result says so.

limit.description: list only: the maximum number of artifacts to return (default 25).

scope.description: list: which listing to return. 'mine' is the default. The others are 'shared', 'all', 'types', 'files' (with `url`) and 'assets' (with `url`, continued with `after`). See **Calls**.

type_query.description: list with scope 'types' only: limits the listing to the types whose title or description match this text best, ignoring case; a type that matches less well is left out, so a narrowed listing is not the whole catalog. Claude omits it when choosing a type for a request, unless a listing made without it says more types exist than it shows.

type.description: list only: the name of a published Artifact type, as a 'types' listing shows it (case does not matter). The listing then shows the Artifacts made from that type instead of the person's gallery. Claude passes this or `type_url`, not both.

intent.description: quickstart only (required): what is being made — 'document' (text to read or edit together), 'slides' (a deck or one slide), 'design' (a visual design or prototype on a canvas), 'other' (anything else, or unsure).

design_systems.description: quickstart only: false when a design system's link is already in hand (it is then read with its own call) or one was declined. Omitted or true, the result lists the design systems (not for a document) and, for slides or a design, attaches the default one's README.

title.description: publish: the fallback title for an HTML page whose file has no <title>. It is a name, not a summary, and Claude keeps it the same across redeploys. On a `type_url` create, it is the new Artifact's name: what the person called it, or a short descriptive name. If it is left out, the Artifact is named after the type.

description.description: publish: one sentence for the subtitle on the gallery card.

label.description: A short name for this publish, at most 60 characters (e.g. "Draft to legal"). Optional. It is a few words, not a description.

overwrite_unread.description: publish with `files` or `root` to an existing artifact: published paths this call may replace or remove although you have not read or listed them in this session. Every other path the call touches must be one you read by its `path`, saw in a file listing, or published yourself, and must not have changed since — otherwise nothing is sent and the refusal names each path. Name a path here only when the user asked for it to be replaced without looking at what is there; it never excuses a path that changed after you read it.

url.description: An existing artifact's claude.ai link (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}); a chat, project or session link is not one, and `action: "list"` lists the person's artifacts. On a publish, it is the artifact to update in place, one the person owns or was given edit access to (a read of it says "writer"). Before publishing to an artifact this conversation has neither read nor published, Claude reads it (`action: "read"`) and builds on what comes back; a publish sent without that read is refused. A refusal that hands Claude the live version counts as that read: Claude merges its changes into that version and publishes the result, and never resends the refused content unchanged. Claude omits `url` for a new artifact or to redeploy a file this conversation already published. For read, delete and the other calls that take a URL, it is the artifact to act on.

type_url.description: publish: the Artifact type to create this new, private Artifact from (a link from a 'types' listing). Claude omits `url`. Any `file_path`/`files` passed become the new Artifact's own files beside the type's fixed ones. read (no `url`): the type to describe. list: the type whose Artifacts to list, or Claude names the type with `type` instead.

auto_open.description: Only with `type_url` and no `file_path`: when the new Artifact opens for the person. Claude passes "after_first_write" when it will fill the Artifact right after creating it with a files publish to its url, so the person does not first see it empty. The Artifact then opens on that first write. Otherwise Claude omits it, and the Artifact opens when created; Claude always omits it for a type whose content it writes through a connector, such as a Claude Docs document, since no publish or store write follows to open it.

prompt.description: read, for an artifact shared with the person: what Claude needs from it, which steers the isolated summary.

force.description: publish: a last-resort overwrite that **discards** the newer published version. On a conflict, Claude merges its changes onto the newer content that the rejection hands it and publishes again. Claude passes true only when the person explicitly said to discard that specific version, and the server may still refuse it over a version saved from inside the page.

out_dir.description: read with `path`: the directory to save into. The default is this artifact's folder in Claude's scratchpad directory, where saving needs no approval. A published file lands at <out_dir>/<published path>, and saving it outside that default folder asks the person first. An asset's file is named by its id plus its type's extension; saving it outside the default folder is an ordinary file save the person may be asked to approve.

path.description: read: the file's published path inside the artifact, exactly as a 'files' listing printed it ("index.html" is the page itself). The file is saved locally, the result says where, and a small text file's contents are included. It can instead be an uploaded asset's id (32 hex characters, from an 'assets' listing or an upload result), and that asset is saved to a local file. delete: the id of the one asset to remove.

paths.description: read: several published paths in place of `path`, up to 256 in one call. Each file is saved as a single `path` would be, and the result lists where each one landed, or why it could not be read, with small text files' contents included while they fit.

after.description: list with scope 'assets' only: the `next` value from a previous listing, passed to continue it.

page.description: read only: true returns the rendered page in cases where a read otherwise returns something else. A typed Artifact's read leaves out the type's own page.

capabilities.description: publish: the runtime capabilities this page declares, as {name: config}. Claude loads the `artifact-capabilities` skill before passing it. On a redeploy Claude omits the field to keep what the page has, and {} clears it.

contract.description: publish: the artifact's runtime version. Leaving it out keeps the current version (the default), 'latest' upgrades, and an exact version pins or rolls back. It changes how the published page behaves, so Claude passes it only when the author explicitly intends that change.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

new_string.description: The text to replace it with (must be different from old_string)

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences of old_string (default false)

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__dismiss_task
tools.description:
Withdraw a background-task chip you previously created with spawn_task.

Call this when a suggestion you flagged is now stale, superseded, or irrelevant — e.g. you (or the user) already fixed it in this session, or you spawned a better-scoped replacement. To replace a chip: call spawn_task with the new suggestion first, then dismiss the old task_id.

Only chips the user hasn't acted on can be withdrawn from the queue. If the user already started or dismissed the task, the result says so (a dismissed task's copy kept for later is withdrawn too) — do not retry.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter
tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__spawn_task
tools.description:
Flag an out-of-scope issue for a separate background task.

Call this when you notice something worth fixing that would bloat the current change — dead code, stale docs, missing coverage, a confirmed TODO, or a security issue spotted in passing. Don't flag vague code-smell observations, trivial fixes you can do inline, or low-confidence hunches. A chip appears for the user; one click spins it off into its own session. Your current turn continues uninterrupted.

The prompt must stand alone — include file paths and enough context to act without this conversation.

The result includes a task_id; call dismiss_task with it if the suggestion later becomes stale.

content.content:
# Nxeon multi-node synergy — full audit + hardening plan

## Context

Nxeon just grew from one Proxmox compute node (primary, OVH Singapore) to two (node-2, Hetzner Falkenstein, onboarded today). Enabling node-2 for real traffic surfaced one confirmed bug (the worker's NAT/port-forward sync only ever touches the primary's own iptables). The owner asked: "the primary node needs to be able to have complete control of all of the nodes, complete sync, am I right?" — yes, and a full platform-wide audit (3 parallel deep-research passes + 1 design pass, all cross-verified against live code) found this is bigger than one bug: **one shared root-cause function** (`lib/sftp.ts`'s `connectionTarget()`) silently breaks nearly the entire SSH-based customer control panel for any server not on the primary node, plus several independent gaps (a live firewall-hardening exposure on node-2 right now, zero disaster-recovery backup coverage for node-2, a backup-download 404-class bug, a stale vmid-collision risk). Zero real customers have ever been provisioned onto node-2 (confirmed via DB), so every fix below can be built and proven safely before it matters to anyone. node-2 is currently `enabled: false` in the DB (disabled earlier today as an immediate protective measure) and should stay that way until Phase 0 + Phase 1 land.

## Ground truth (verified against live code and the live host, not assumed)

- **Architecture**: `Node` model (schema.prisma:1151) — one row per physical Proxmox host (`apiUrl`/`tokenId`/`tokenSecret`/`publicIp`/`natChain`/`bridge`/`subnetPrefix`/`provider`/`region`). VM-level operations are ALREADY correctly multi-node via `pveFor`/`pveForNode` (lib/proxmox.ts) — that part of today's earlier rollout is solid. There is exactly ONE worker process for the whole platform (`worker/index.ts`, systemd unit `nxeon-worker`), running only on the primary — confirmed via package.json, CLAUDE.md, and `onboard-node.sh`'s own header, which already documents each node as a separate NAT island with no cross-node private networking.
- **Bug Class A (pure code fix, no new infra)**: `lib/sftp.ts:35-41` (`SftpServer` type) has no `node` field; `connectionTarget()` (~line 137) resolves a non-dedicated-IP server's SSH host as `process.env.PUBLIC_IP` (the primary's IP), never `server.node.publicIp`. Verified live — the type and doc comment match exactly. This one function underpins `lib/ssh-exec.ts`'s `withServerSsh()`/`exec()` and `lib/sftp.ts`'s `withSftp()`, which are the shared SSH plumbing for: the web terminal, file manager, game console/RCON/kick/ban, game power/backup/scheduled-restart/player-tracking (worker sweeps firing every ~60s), the cPanel-lite control panel (websites/DBs/services/one-click apps/static-site publish), SSL issuance, game mods/config, the guest-side half of disk-expand/volume-attach, migration data-copy, the fleet SSH-health sweep (fires every ~15min), and the free-Minecraft shared host. Two call sites already do this correctly and prove the fix pattern: `worker/index.ts:712,814` and `worker/game-subdomain-sync.ts`'s `resolveGameServerDnsTarget()`. `worker/volumes.ts` and `worker/disk-expand.ts` **already select `node`** for their Proxmox calls — they self-heal for free the moment the root fix lands. Three files (`worker/claude.ts`, `worker/game-update.ts`, `worker/firewall.ts`) bypass `connectionTarget` entirely with an even more broken pattern (direct dial to the guest's *private* `10.20.x.x` IP, which the primary has no route to for node-2) — these fold into the same fix once rewritten onto `withServerSsh`.
- **Bug Class B (needs new infrastructure — the worker has no OS-level access to a second physical machine)**: (1) `worker/network.ts`'s `syncPortForwards()`/`reconcileNatChain()` rebuilds NAT/DNAT iptables rules via local `execFile("iptables",...)` — only ever the primary's kernel. (2) `worker/index.ts`'s `provision()` writes the per-VM cloud-init vendor snippet via local `fs.writeFile()` — a VM provisioned on node-2 is told to read a snippet that only ever landed on the primary's disk, so it boots and reports "ready" while its setup script silently never ran. (3) `lib/dedicated-ip.ts`'s `hasLiveDnatRule()` checks the primary's local iptables before allocating a dedicated IP — for a node-2 IP this checks the wrong host, risking a double-allocation.
- **Separate, independent bugs**: `lib/monitoring.ts`'s `backupSummary()` merges every node's backup listing into one scalar, so a healthy primary backup masks a silently-broken node-2 backup schedule forever (sibling function `nodeStorageUsage()` in the same file already does this correctly, per-node, unmerged — copy that shape). `lib/platform-backups.ts` (admin disaster-recovery panel) reads only local files on whichever box the web app runs on — zero node-2 awareness, and the *customer*-backup half of that same admin page already has the correct per-node loop + "some nodes unreachable" honesty banner to copy. `app/api/servers/[id]/backups/download/route.ts` checks tenancy correctly per-node but then reads the archive bytes from a hardcoded local path — 502s for every node-2 server's backup download. At least one `Server` row (`minecraft-mm8w85`, confirmed in docs/QA-PRELAUNCH.md) has `nodeId: null`, which is a live vmid-collision risk now that a second node genuinely exists.
- **Firewall — corrected finding, better news than first suspected**: the primary already runs a mature, incident-hardened system, confirmed live and running right now: `nxeon-firewall.service` (active), `fail2ban.service` (active), `scripts/firewall.nft`, `scripts/admin-ip.sh`, `scripts/firewall-safe-apply.sh`, `scripts/firewall-reachability.sh`. None of it was ever packaged into `scripts/onboard-node.sh` or checked into `deploy/` as an installable unit template — so node-2 almost certainly has none of it. This is "port a proven system," not "build one from scratch."
- **Security-posture precedent already in this codebase**: `Node` deliberately has no SSH fields (only a scoped API token), unlike the separate `HostingNode` model which does have SSH fields for a different product with a different trust model. `lib/telemetry-token.ts`'s `mintTelemetryToken()`/hash-stored-not-plaintext pattern is the existing precedent for minting a new per-entity bearer credential.

## Decisions

- **Class B gets a lightweight per-node HTTP agent with its own bearer token — not SSH.** This preserves the existing "every physical host is reached via a narrow, token-authenticated API" invariant (matching `Node`'s existing Proxmox-token design, not `HostingNode`'s SSH design), keeps the blast radius of a leaked credential to ~6 named operations instead of an arbitrary root shell, and slots directly into `lib/nat-rules.ts`'s already-built-and-tested `NatHost` interface (`ensureChain`/`listChain`/`addRule`/`deleteRule`) with zero changes to the tested reconciliation logic in `reconcileNatChain()` — only a new transport implementation.
- **Firewall remediation ships first, out-of-band from the staged rollout** — it's a live exposure, not an architecture gap, and the fix is "copy 4 scripts + 1 systemd unit," not new engineering.
- **`nodeId: null` backfill ships first too** — one-time, low-risk, fully decoupled from everything else.
- **Both documentation deliverables are written incrementally as each phase lands**, not once at the end — matching this repo's own stated convention that docs update in the same commit as the change.
- **node-2 stays `enabled: false`** until Phase 0 and Phase 1 are live and verified against a real throwaway test server.

## Phase 0 — Immediate, today, out-of-band from everything else

1. **Firewall port to node-2**: copy `firewall.nft`, `admin-ip.sh`, `firewall-safe-apply.sh`, `firewall-reachability.sh` + install `fail2ban` + `/etc/fail2ban/jail.d/nxeon.conf` onto node-2. Seed `/etc/nxeon/admin-ips.nft` from the primary's populated list. **Deliberate posture difference from the primary**: the primary intentionally leaves SSH (22) public (fail2ban-protected only) as a recovery channel of last resort for its public web app; node-2 is a pure compute node with no such need, so set its admin-allowlist to cover **both** 22 and 8006. Document this reasoning inline in the ported script so it reads as a decision. Apply via `firewall-safe-apply.sh`'s full `--check`/`--apply`/verify-from-fresh-connection/`--confirm` flow — never a raw `nft -f`.
2. **`nodeId: null` backfill**: find every `Server` with `nodeId: null`, confirm each vmid is genuinely live on the primary's `pveNode` via the Proxmox API, set `nodeId` to the primary's id. Model the script on `scripts/backfill-claude.ts`'s shape.
3. **Write both documentation deliverables' initial version now** (see Documentation section below) — the retrospective can be written in full immediately (it's describing completed work); the permanent reference doc gets its skeleton + sections 1-2 now, filled in further as each later phase lands.

## Phase 1 — Class A root fix + highest-value call sites

1. Fix `lib/sftp.ts`: add `node?: { publicIp: string } | null` to `SftpServer`; change `connectionTarget()`'s non-dedicated branch to `server.node?.publicIp ?? process.env.PUBLIC_IP ?? ""`. Keep `node` optional (preserves today's exact fallback behavior for any row that's genuinely primary-only).
2. Verify `worker/volumes.ts`/`worker/disk-expand.ts` self-heal (no code change — they already select `node`).
3. Thread `node: { select: { publicIp: true } }` into the query for, in order: `worker/ssh-health.ts` (stops false fleet-wide alerts first), `lib/actions-game-control.ts` + `worker/game-control.ts` (highest-frequency customer surface), `terminal-server/index.ts` + `lib/actions-files.ts` + `app/api/files/[serverId]/route.ts` (web terminal + file manager).
4. Prove the pattern end-to-end against a real throwaway test server provisioned on node-2 before moving to Phase 2.

## Phase 2 — Remaining Class A sites + the 3 rewrites + backupSummary (parallelizable)

1. `worker/websites.ts`'s shared `sshServer()` (fixes it + `site-publish.ts` + `apps.ts` for free), `worker/databases.ts`, `worker/services.ts`, `worker/ssl.ts`.
2. `worker/game-mods.ts` (currently inert, behind `ENABLE_REAL_GAMEMODS`) + `worker/game-config.ts` (type + trace to the underlying query).
3. `lib/claude-backfill.ts` / `scripts/backfill-claude.ts`, `lib/actions-free-minecraft.ts`'s `freemcHost()` (1-line, removes a landmine even though not exercised until that host moves).
4. Rewrite `worker/claude.ts`, `worker/game-update.ts`, `worker/firewall.ts` onto `withServerSsh`/`exec` (do this after at least one Tier-3 file from Phase 1 is proven against real node-2 traffic). Note `lib/ssh-exec.ts`'s `exec()` returns `{code,stdout,stderr}` rather than throwing — adjust each file's error handling accordingly; preserve each file's existing secret-redaction logic.
5. `lib/monitoring.ts`'s `backupSummary()`: change to return per-node results (copy `nodeStorageUsage()`'s shape in the same file, don't merge). Update its two callers (`app/admin/monitoring/page.tsx`, `worker/monitor.ts`'s staleness check) to alert per-node — add a `BACKUP` dimension to `lib/node-capacity.ts`'s existing `CapDimension` enum and route through the existing `NodeAlert` debounce/resolve machinery rather than inventing a second alerting path. This item has no dependency on the node-agent and can land any time in this window.
6. Save `worker/migrate.ts`/`migrate-real.ts`'s `connectTarget()` fix for last in this phase given the file's size and that migrations touch live customer data mid-flight — test via `scripts/migration-rehearsal.ts` before trusting it against a real customer migration onto a node-2 destination.

## Phase 3 — Node-agent build (Class B), can start day 1 in parallel with Phase 1/2 (zero file overlap)

1. New `node-agent/` service (parallel to `terminal-server/`), small HTTP(S) server. New `deploy/nxeon-node-agent.service` template.
2. Schema: `Node.agentTokenHash String?` (mint/hash pattern copied from `lib/telemetry-token.ts`, raw token shown once, stored as SHA-256 hash).
3. Endpoints (bearer auth, one primitive per `NatHost` method — keeps the tested reconciliation logic on the primary): `GET /v1/health`; `POST /v1/nat/ensure-chain`; `GET /v1/nat/chain/:chain`; `POST /v1/nat/rule` / `DELETE /v1/nat/rule` (reuse `NatRule` from `lib/nat-rules.ts` verbatim); `POST /v1/snippet` + `DELETE /v1/snippet/:filename` (filename allowlisted); `GET /v1/iptables/dnat-check?address=X`.
4. Dispatch helper (e.g. `natHostFor(node)` in `worker/network.ts`): local `iptablesHost()` when `node.isPrimary`, else an HTTP-backed `agentNatHost(node)` adapter implementing the same `NatHost` interface. The primary itself never runs the agent.
5. Network exposure: agent bound to the node's public IP, gated by that node's own nftables to accept connections only from the primary's public IP (same single-source-allow mechanism `admin-ip.sh` already implements for 8006 — a new set, not the human admin allowlist).
6. Admin UI: extend `/admin/nodes/new`, `addNode()`/`updateNode()` (lib/actions-nodes.ts) with an agent-token field (hashed immediately, never redisplayed); extend `testNode()` to also probe `GET /v1/health`.
7. Extend `scripts/onboard-node.sh` with a new step: ship the bundled agent, generate+write the token (0600), install+enable the systemd unit, add the primary's IP to the node's agent-port allowlist, print the token in the same "Add node" form block the script already prints.
8. Wire real callers: `worker/network.ts` (NAT sync), `worker/index.ts`'s `provision()` (snippet write), `lib/dedicated-ip.ts`'s `hasLiveDnatRule()` (dnat-check) — each dispatches to the agent only for non-primary nodes.
9. Real end-to-end test: provision a throwaway NAT-based game server on node-2, confirm `iptables -t nat -S NXEON_FWD` on node-2 itself shows the rule, then prove it externally (connect from a third machine to node-2's public IP). Confirm a fresh node-2 provision actually ran its setup script (MOTD/guest-agent/telemetry shipper present).

## Phase 4 — Agent-dependent bugs

1. Extend the agent with `GET /v1/backup/:filename` (stream bytes, reuse the download route's existing `ARCHIVE_RE`/basename-confinement checks) and `GET /v1/backup-status`.
2. Fix the backup-download 502: branch on `server.node?.isPrimary` in the download route.
3. Fix `lib/platform-backups.ts`: loop all nodes, merge into a per-node view, render with the exact "some nodes unreachable" honesty-banner pattern already used in `app/admin/backups/page.tsx`'s customer-backup section.

## Phase 5 — Backlog (not blocking, no customer impact today)

- OsTemplate drift-verification sweep (diff each node's template vmid list against the primary's, alert on mismatch) rather than new sync infrastructure.
- Consolidate the duplicated `sshServer()` helpers (websites/databases/services) into one shared export, now that all three have been touched anyway.
- WireGuard/VXLAN mesh for cross-node private VM networking — only if a future feature actually needs guest-to-guest connectivity across nodes.

## Documentation (write incrementally, per CLAUDE.md's existing "docs update in the same commit" rule)

**(a) Retrospective — expand the existing `docs/DOCUMENTATION.md` section "Onboarding a Hetzner dedicated node via rescue-mode QEMU install (2026-09-05)"** into a broader "Multi-node rollout" heading that keeps the two physical-install gotchas + template-parity note verbatim and adds: motivation/timeline; schema changes (`Node`, `Server.nodeId`, `DedicatedIp.nodeId`, contrast with `HostingNode`); admin UI + monitoring/dashboard changes already shipped earlier today; this audit's Class A/B findings and the separate bugs; what shipped in each phase and when; generalizable lessons for node #3+. Write this one now, in full — it describes completed work.

**(b) Permanent reference — new section in `docs/DOCUMENTATION.md`, "How multi-node synergy works + how to add node N"**, cross-referenced from the existing single-node "Architecture at a glance" diagram: (1) why multi-node exists + the NAT-island principle; (2) the `Node` model field-by-field vs `HostingNode`; (3) the node-agent — purpose/endpoints/auth/token location; (4) the standing rule that any new per-server Proxmox call must go through `pveFor`/`pveForNode`; (5) the `connectionTarget()` choke point + a checklist that any new SSH/SFTP call site must select both `dedicatedIp` and `node`; (6) a narrative "add node N" runbook derived from `onboard-node.sh`'s actual steps including the new firewall + agent steps; (7) known limitations (no cross-node private VM networking, no template-drift verification). Start this now with sections 1-2-6(partial); fill in 3-4-5-7 as Phases 1-4 land.

## Critical files

- `lib/sftp.ts` — Class A root-cause fix, unlocks ~18 downstream files
- `worker/network.ts` + `lib/nat-rules.ts` — Class B's NAT-sync fix and the `NatHost` seam the node-agent implements against
- `worker/index.ts` — `provision()`'s snippet-write bug (Class B), the `nodeFor()` fallback pattern
- `scripts/onboard-node.sh` — where the firewall port and the node-agent install both get added; determines whether node #3 inherits every fix automatically
- `prisma/schema.prisma` — `Node.agentTokenHash` addition
- `lib/monitoring.ts` — `backupSummary()`/`nodeStorageUsage()` (the fix pattern to copy)
- `lib/platform-backups.ts`, `app/api/servers/[id]/backups/download/route.ts`, `app/admin/backups/page.tsx` — Phase 4's three related fixes, sharing one reference UI pattern
- `docs/QA-PRELAUNCH.md`, `docs/MIGRATION.md`, `docs/DOCUMENTATION.md` — where the audit's own findings are already partially tracked and where both documentation deliverables live

## Verification

- **Unit-level**: extend `connectionTarget()`'s tests with "node present → node.publicIp wins" and "node absent → falls back to PUBLIC_IP" (regression guard for the primary's existing fleet). Test the agent's `NatHost` adapter's HTTP serialization only (the reconciliation logic itself is already fully covered by `test/nat-sync.test.ts` against an in-memory fake) — use `undici`'s `MockAgent`.
- **Real-node integration** (safe today — zero real customers on node-2): provision one throwaway plain VPS and one throwaway NAT game server directly on node-2. After Phase 1: confirm web terminal, file manager, and `ssh-health.ts` stop false-alarming against it. After Phase 2: confirm game console/RCON/backup/mods/config all work. After Phase 3: confirm the NAT rule appears on node-2's own iptables AND is reachable externally; confirm a fresh provision's setup script actually ran. After Phase 4: stop the node-2 agent momentarily and confirm `/admin/backups`/`/admin/monitoring` show an honesty banner instead of silently looking fine.
- **Firewall**: run `firewall-reachability.sh` against node-2's candidate ruleset before applying; use `firewall-safe-apply.sh`'s full deadman-switch flow, never a raw `nft -f`.
- **Regression safety for the ~150+ existing primary servers**: the fix is additive/optional (`node` stays nullable) — no unmodified file's behavior changes until its query is touched. Spot-check each Tier-3 file against a couple of real *existing* primary servers immediately after editing it.
- Only re-enable `node-2` (`enabled: true`) once Phase 0 + Phase 1 are verified.

input.prompt:
Read-only audit in the git worktree /opt/nxeon-wt-concur (a Next.js + Prisma repo). Do NOT edit anything. Search breadth: very thorough.

Context: `lib/sftp.ts` exports `connectionTarget(server)` which resolves a server's SSH host as `server.dedicatedIp?.address` if dedicated, else `server.node?.publicIp ?? process.env.PUBLIC_IP`. The platform now has 5 Proxmox nodes, so any caller that passes a Server object WITHOUT selecting `node: { select: { publicIp: true } }` (and `dedicatedIp: { select: { address: true } }`) will dial the wrong physical host for servers on non-primary nodes. Also `guestSshPort` and `sshManagementKeyEnc` should be selected where available.

Task: find EVERY call site of `withServerSsh(`, `withSftp(`, `connectionTarget(`, `listDir(`/`statPath(`/`readFileText(`/`writeFileText(`/`readFileBuffer(`/`writeFileBuffer(`/`mkdirPath(`/`renamePath(`/`removePath(`/`chmodPath(` from lib/sftp.ts, plus any direct `new Client()` from `ssh2` or `ssh2-sftp-client` or `spawn('ssh'|'sshpass'|'scp'...)` that dials a customer server — across `worker/**`, `lib/**`, `terminal-server/**`, `app/api/**`, `app/**/actions*.ts`, `scripts/**`. For each call site, trace back to the Prisma query that produced the server object (it may be in another function/file, e.g. a `loadServer`/`sshServer()` helper or `db.server.findUnique/findFirst/findMany`) and report:
- file:line of the call site
- file:line of the query that loads the server
- whether the query selects/includes `node` (publicIp), `dedicatedIp`, `guestSshPort`, `sshManagementKeyEnc`, `rootPasswordEnc`  (yes/no each). If the query uses no `select`/`include` at all (so returns all scalar columns but NO relations), say "scalars only — node and dedicatedIp MISSING".

import type { Prisma } from "@prisma/client";
import { db } from "./db";

/**
 * Serialise "is a job already in flight for this server? if not, enqueue one"
 * per server, across every web process.
 *
 * WHY THIS EXISTS (found 2026-09-30, reproduced on staging): the "one in-flight
 * job per server" guard in `serverAction` (lib/actions.ts) and `gamePower`
 * (lib/actions-game-control.ts) was a plain `count()` followed by a separate
 * `create()`. Two requests landing within the same few milliseconds both saw
 * zero in-flight jobs and both enqueued — 10 simultaneous Reboot requests
 * against one staging VPS produced 3 REBOOT jobs, and 10 simultaneous game
 * Restarts produced 2 GAME_POWER jobs. A single browser tab can't hit this
 * (Next.js dispatches one Server Action at a time per client), but two tabs, a
 * double-submitting script or a flaky retrying proxy can — and a duplicate
 * START on an already-running VM fails in Proxmox, which after three attempts
 * flips the server to ERROR even though nothing is actually wrong.
 *
 * Wrapping the check + enqueue in a transaction that first takes a
 * transaction-scoped Postgres advisory lock keyed on the server id makes the
 * second request wait until the first has committed its job, so its own count
 * then sees it and it is refused like any other overlapping click. The lock
 * releases automatically on commit/rollback.
 *
 * Key: the two-int form `(namespace, hashtext(serverId))`. Postgres keeps the
 * two-int and single-bigint advisory key spaces separate, so this can never
 * collide with lib/ipam.ts's single-key allocator lock; a hashtext collision
 * between two server ids only means those two servers briefly serialise, never
 * a wrong answer. `pg_advisory_xact_lock` returns `void`, which Prisma's
 * $queryRaw can't deserialize — hence the subselect (same workaround ipam.ts
 * documents).
 */
const SERVER_JOB_LOCK_NAMESPACE = 7301;
const LOCK_SQL = `SELECT 1 AS locked FROM (SELECT pg_advisory_xact_lock(${SERVER_JOB_LOCK_NAMESPACE}, hashtext($1))) _lock`;

export async function withServerJobLock<T>(
  serverId: string,
  fn: (tx: Prisma.TransactionClient) => Promise<T>,
): Promise<T> {
  return db.$transaction(async (tx) => {
    await tx.$queryRawUnsafe(LOCK_SQL, serverId);
    return fn(tx);
  });
}

## Job lifecycle — the worker queue

`worker/index.ts` is one `for(;;)` loop. It runs housekeeping sweeps on timers, then claims exactly
one job, runs it to completion, and loops. `POLL_MS = 3000` and `MAX_ATTEMPTS = 3` at
`/opt/nxeon/worker/index.ts:34`.

```
                       ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
   server action  ────►│ Job { status: QUEUED, attempts: 0 }     │
                       └───────────────┬─────────────────────────┘
                                       │
  worker/index.ts:1136  findFirst({ status: QUEUED }, orderBy: createdAt asc)
                                       │
  worker/index.ts:1144  ATOMIC CLAIM
         updateMany({ where: { id, status: QUEUED },
                      data:  { status: RUNNING, attempts: { increment: 1 } } })
         claim.count === 1 ? it is mine : another worker took it, re-poll
                                       │
                                       ▼
  worker/index.ts:771   handlers[job.type]     ── 35 JobTypes, one function each
                                       │
              ┌────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────┐
              │ resolved               │ threw                   │
              ▼                        ▼                         │
     status: DONE            attempts < MAX_ATTEMPTS (3)?        │
     progress: 100            ├─ yes → back to QUEUED ───────────┘  retry
     Notification row         └─ no  → status: FAILED
                                        ├─ reconcileFailedJob()   unwinds money
                                        └─ if type ∈ VM_STATE_FAILURE_JOBS
                                                server.status = ERROR
```

`VM_STATE_FAILURE_JOBS` (`/opt/nxeon/worker/index.ts:49`) lists the job types whose failure genuinely
leaves the VM in a bad run or disk state, and therefore the only ones permitted to mark the server
`ERROR`:

```
PROVISION  REINSTALL  DELETE  RESIZE  START  STOP  REBOOT  SUSPEND
UNSUSPEND  BACKUP_RESTORE  SNAPSHOT_ROLLBACK
```

Two deliberate absences, both of them bug fixes:

- **`BACKUP_CREATE` is absent.** Backups run `mode: "snapshot"` and never stop the VM. A customer
  reported "I tried creating a backup but it just shut down the server"; the fix was to stop
  treating a failed backup as a VM-state failure.
- **`DISK_EXPAND` is absent.** Growing a disk cannot change the run state, so a failed expansion
  must leave the server exactly as `RUNNING`/`STOPPED` as it was. Its money is unwound by
  `reconcileFailedJob` instead. Comment at `/opt/nxeon/worker/index.ts:44`.

The 35 job types, grouped:

| Group | Job types |
|---|---|
| Lifecycle | `PROVISION` `START` `STOP` `REBOOT` `REINSTALL` `DELETE` `PASSWORD_RESET` |
| Billing-driven | `SUSPEND` `UNSUSPEND` |
| Capacity | `RESIZE` `DISK_EXPAND` |
| Data protection | `SNAPSHOT_CREATE` `SNAPSHOT_DELETE` `SNAPSHOT_ROLLBACK` `BACKUP_CREATE` `BACKUP_RESTORE` |
| Volumes | `VOLUME_CREATE` `VOLUME_ATTACH` `VOLUME_DETACH` `VOLUME_DELETE` |
| Control panel | `WEBSITE_CREATE` `WEBSITE_DELETE` `WEBSITE_TOGGLE` `WEBSITE_SSL` `DB_CREATE` `DB_DELETE` `APP_INSTALL` `CRON_SYNC` `SERVICE_ACTION` |
| Game control panel | `GAME_POWER` (start/stop/restart the game service) `GAME_BACKUP` (world/save archive) |
| Other subsystems | `SSL_ISSUE` `MIGRATE` `GAME_CONFIG` `GAME_UPDATE` `CLAUDE_BUILD` `SYNC_FORWARDS` |

Sweeps, all registered inline in `main()` at `/opt/nxeon/worker/index.ts:1134`:

| Sweep | Interval | Function | Registered at |
|---|---|---|---|
| Renewals, auto-charge, dunning | 10 min | `billingSweep()` | `:1156` (`worker/billing.ts`) |
| Add-on product renewals | 10 min | `productRenewalSweep()` | `:1162` (`worker/product-renewals.ts`) |
| Visit geo-enrichment | 90 s | `geoEnrichSweep()` | `:1180` (`worker/geo.ts`) |
| Scheduled customer backups | 15 min | `scheduledBackupSweep()` | `:1188` (`worker/backup-schedule.ts`) |
| SSL renewal + reconcile | 30 min | `sslSweep()` | `:1208` (`worker/ssl.ts`) |
| **Post-cutover migration TLS** | 30 min | `postCutoverTlsSweep()` | `:1216` (`worker/migrate.ts`) — **not** covered by `sslSweep`; a migration writes no `SslCertificate` row |
| Monitoring alerts | 10 min | `monitorSweep()` | `:1224` (`worker/monitor.ts`) |
| Abuse detection | 10 min | `abuseSweep()` | `:1229` (`worker/abuse.ts`) |
| In-guest disk sampling | 10 min | `sampleServerDisks()` | `:1236` (`worker/monitor.ts`) |
| Dedicated-IP pool import | 5 min | `syncDedicatedIpPool()` | `:1245` (`lib/dedicated-ip.ts`) |
| Game auto-update | 6 h | `gameUpdateSweep()` | `:1171` (`worker/game-update.ts`) |
| Game scheduled restarts | 60 s | `gameScheduleSweep()` | `worker/game-control.ts` — fires due `GameSchedule` rows as `GAME_POWER` restarts |

Every sweep is individually `try`/`catch`ed with a `console.error`, so one failing sweep cannot stop
the loop — but that also means a permanently broken sweep is invisible outside the journal. When
something scheduled has quietly stopped happening, grep the journal for `sweep error`.

## Environments — production, staging, and the .env contract

export const UPTIME_SWEEP_MS = 5 * 60_000;

/** Statuses where the server is not expected to be up, so sampling it would
 *  record a false outage. A stopped VM is the customer's choice, not downtime;
 *  a provisioning one has not started existing yet. */
const NOT_MEASURED = new Set(["PENDING", "PROVISIONING", "REINSTALLING", "DELETING", "STOPPED", "ERROR"]);

export async function sweepUptime(): Promise<{ sampled: number; up: number; failed: number }> {
  const servers = await db.server.findMany({
    where: { vmid: { not: null }, status: { notIn: [...NOT_MEASURED] as never } },
    select: { id: true, vmid: true },
  });

  let up = 0;
  let sampled = 0;
  let failed = 0;

  for (const s of servers) {
    if (s.vmid == null) continue;
    try {
      const st = await vmStatus(s.vmid);
      const isUp = st?.status === "running";
      await recordSample(s.id, isUp);
      sampled++;
      if (isUp) up++;
    } catch {
      // An API error is OUR blind spot, not the customer's outage. Recording a
      // down sample here would blame the customer's server for our inability to
      // reach the hypervisor — so the sample is dropped and the day's `total`
      // simply does not grow.
      failed++;
    }
  }
  return { sampled, up, failed };
}

The changelog placement looks good, so now I'm planning the implementation order, starting with schema changes: adding startedAt and finishedAt fields to the Job model to track timing, deciding priority doesn't need its own schema field since it can be derived from job type.

I'll also add indexes on (status, createdAt) and (type, finishedAt) to support the claim queries and metrics efficiently. Next comes the scheduling logic in worker/scheduler.ts with per-node and per-type caps plus fairness logic, a separate SweepRunner for background sweeps with overlap guards and timeouts, updates to worker/index.ts for graceful shutdown and metrics writes, a job-metrics module computing p50/p95 latencies via raw SQL percentile queries, request timeout and caching for Proxmox status calls, node-aware updates across uptime and cron/marketing code paths, and finally tests covering the new scheduler behavior.

Writing priority and job type definitions...

I'm reconsidering where PROVISION should fall in priority — it's customer-facing and feels instant-ish, so it probably needs higher priority than true bulk jobs like backups, even though it's not strictly in the interactive set.

For concurrency limits, I'm thinking I'll raise WORKER_CONCURRENCY to 16 since interactive jobs are lightweight, and set per-node caps: a heavy-operation cap of 3 per node, a total of 8 per node, and a global bulk cap of 4 so bulk jobs don't flood the queue — though I'll confirm these numbers after running the load test.

For fairness, I'm considering a per-user running cap of max(2, concurrency/4), using round-robin ordering among candidates sorted by priority then by how much that user already has running, so one user bulk-submitting many provisions doesn't starve others, while still letting them use idle capacity when nobody else is waiting.

Then, after the main pass, I claim from the deferred list in order, still respecting hard caps. I define "heavy" job types as those stressing node storage—provisioning, reinstall, backup operations, resize, disk expand, snapshots, delete, volume ops, migrate—with a default per-node heavy cap of 3 and total cap of 6, using nodeId (or "primary" fallback) as the grouping key, with nodeless jobs excluded from counts. I'm designing selectClaims as a pure function taking candidates and active entries as input.

A failed CAS during claim attempts just gets skipped for that tick, which is slightly conservative but acceptable, and successful claims record a startedAt timestamp. Now I'm sketching out a SweepRunner class for the worker that registers named sweeps with intervals, timeouts, and concurrency limits, running each on its own loop.

For timeouts I can't truly cancel the underlying promise, but I can release its semaphore slot and log an overrun, gating the next run behind an overlap guard flag; default timeout is 5 minutes with a concurrency cap of 3, and scheduling considers an initial delay plus jitter so sweeps stagger at boot rather than firing simultaneously.

Since `lastSweep = 0` makes everything due immediately on first loop, the semaphore naturally throttles them to 3 concurrent; next runs are scheduled as interval-after-completion to avoid pile-up. For graceful shutdown, I'm setting a draining flag on SIGTERM/SIGINT that stops new claims, waits for active jobs up to a configurable drain timeout, then requeues any still-running jobs by decrementing their attempts and clearing errors so they're restart-neutral.

For crash recovery at startup, reapStuckJobs requeues without burning a real attempt, but I need to guard against infinite crash loops — I'm considering tracking an interruption counter in the payload (using an underscore-prefixed key like `_restarts` to avoid colliding with handler-read fields) and marking the job FAILED after repeated interruptions. I should spot-check whether any handlers validate payload shape strictly before adding this field, and also think through whether PROVISION is safely re-entrant if killed mid-execution.

Checking that logic, the vmid-persisted-before-clone pattern means a re-check should skip the clone step if the VM already exists, though there's an edge case where a half-cloned VM with a Proxmox lock could still be mid-task — acceptable given retry/waitForTask handling elsewhere, and still better than failing outright.

For the retry path I'm also deciding how timestamps should work: finishedAt only gets set on terminal status, startedAt stays fixed at first claim (not reset on retry), so queue wait is measured from createdAt to first startedAt, and total run time including retries is startedAt to finishedAt.

I'm now tackling the big edit to worker/index.ts's main() function, rewriting it along with reapStuckJobs and runJob's finishedAt handling. I need to carefully preserve each sweep registration with its interval—like the promo-reservations sweep running every 2 minutes—while restructuring them through the SweepRunner.

Working through the remaining sweeps: billing runs every 10 minutes with commission reconciliation after renewals, renewal reminders hourly, google-ads every 15 minutes, uptime on its own configured interval, ssh-health every 15 minutes with a 10 minute timeout, vm-recovery every 5 minutes, and various game, tracking, and geo sweeps running on shorter cycles. Then there's the hosting cluster of sweeps—provisioning, database, task, health checks, SSL, hardening, telemetry—plus nxcloud, SSL renewal, and monitoring sweeps that bundle things like disk/memory sampling and abuse detection, and I'm deciding whether to keep those as separate registrations or consolidate them.

Beyond that I'm cataloging the marketing-related sweeps (outreach, SEO, winback sequences, cold email flows, ticket/DM digests) and IP pool sync, which I want to move out of its inline body into its own function. I'm now sketching the main loop to use selectClaims for claiming work with graceful shutdown handling, and noting that runJob needs to set finishedAt when a job reaches DONE or failed state.

For claiming jobs atomically, since Prisma's updateMany can't conditionally set startedAt only if null, I'm writing a raw SQL CAS query that updates status, increments attempts, and uses COALESCE to preserve an existing startedAt while setting it on first run, filtering on QUEUED status and casting the enum properly.

For stuck job recovery: I'll requeue RUNNING jobs without burning an attempt, decrementing attempts back down, while tracking a `_restarts` counter in the payload; once it hits 3 I'll mark the job FAILED with a clear message about repeated restarts, reusing the existing failure path and logging. The graceful drain on exit should mark jobs the same way so the reaper finds nothing to recover on next boot. For the payload merge, I need to guard against non-object payloads (strings/arrays) and only merge the restart counter in when it's a plain object, otherwise just leave it alone without tracking.

Now I'm designing the shutdown sequence: set draining flag, stop the sweep loop, wait up to a drain timeout (balancing systemd's default stop timeout against a safer value), then for any jobs still active, bulk-update them from RUNNING back to QUEUED with attempts decremented but floored at zero using a raw SQL clamp, and finally exit the process cleanly.

I'm also reasoning through race conditions during shutdown—if a job completes between the requeue update and process exit, the completion write overwrites QUEUED with DONE harmlessly, but if the handler is mid-flight at exit, the row stays QUEUED and gets retried by another worker, which only works safely if the handler is idempotent (true for PROVISION). I'm flagging that server-level status shouldn't be reverted, and that risky non-idempotent job types like RESIZE or DISK_EXPAND need special handling to avoid double side effects like double billing.

I'm narrowing down a "safe to auto-resume" allowlist of job types—things like PROVISION, REINSTALL, DELETE, backups, syncs, power actions, password resets, SSL issuance, and snapshots—while excluding jobs with their own run-state tracking like MIGRATE or anything that charges a wallet without idempotency guarantees.

Actually, rethinking it: a cleaner rule might be to requeue all job types on restart without burning an attempt, since a restart isn't the job's fault, capped at under three restarts. But I need to check whether money-charging handlers like resize could double-charge on a re-run, so I'm going to grep for debitWallet usage there.

That's denied, so I'll mark it as needing the owner to run manually and move on without retrying. Now I'm planning the loadtest harness, using WorkerLoop from worker/index.ts with sandbox flags set against the throwaway DB, and generating fake handler durations sampled from a distribution modeled on real traffic.

Since queue wait pollutes the createdAt→updatedAt timing, I'm using p25 per job type over the last two weeks as a proxy for actual run time, giving rough estimates like PROVISION ~240s, GAME_POWER ~20s, GAME_CONFIG ~30s, BACKUP_CREATE ~120s, and REBOOT ~27s. The harness will accept scenario size, concurrency, caps, and a time-compression speed factor, then seed users and servers across fake nodes, create corresponding Job rows, and run WorkerLoop against these fake handlers.

For comparing against legacy behavior, I'm planning to make the claim-selection function injectable into WorkerLoopOptions so the harness can swap in a simple FIFO selector with concurrency 8 and per-server locking only, instead of the priority-aware scheduler, to emulate the old system faithfully.

Next I need to figure out the fake data setup — Job rows reference Server via FK, and Server rows need userId, planId, osTemplateId, and nodeId, so I have to check the required fields on the Server and Node models before writing the harness, and also verify how the sandbox flag reads the NXEON_SANDBOX environment variable.

content.thinking:
I'm modeling runtime durations for each operation type as lognormal distributions around realistic medians, then starting to design the test harness with an environment flag to control worker execution behavior.

I need the harness to refuse running against the production database, requiring an explicit sandbox flag and throwaway database URL. I'm planning to seed test data (nodes, users, servers, plans) and burst-create jobs simultaneously, then run the worker loop with fake handlers that sleep for sampled durations, polling until all jobs complete so I can report queue wait and run time percentiles by type and priority, plus a legacy mode that emulates inline sweep stalls for comparison.

For scenarios, I'm designing a `--scenario burst:N` flag that creates N simultaneous provisions, restarts, and config applies alongside background backup/update traffic, with configurable bulk size, user distribution including a "hog" user to test fairness, round-robin node assignment, and a `--matrix` flag to run multiple configurations and compare results alongside the scheduler limits used.

Working through the timing math, I settle on a default simulation speed of 30x so a 100-provision run with 5 nodes completes in under a minute of wall time, making the full matrix of comparisons feasible to run in the background within a few minutes.

Checking that importing worker/index.ts doesn't trigger unwanted side effects at module load—env reads are fine, and main() is properly guarded by the no-main flag. I need to make sure seeded Job rows reference the server's nodeId correctly, then write the implementation along with the select option in index.ts.
