## Job lifecycle — the worker queue

`worker/index.ts` is one process (systemd `nxeon-worker`) but, since 2026-10-01, two independent
things run inside it: a **claim loop** whose only job is to pick QUEUED `Job` rows and run them
concurrently (`WorkerLoop`), and a **sweep runner** (`worker/sweeps.ts`) that runs every housekeeping
sweep on its own timer. The two never wait on each other — that separation is the fix for the
six-minute "Applying…" a customer sat through on 2026-10-01 while the old single loop was busy inside
`ssh-health` + `player-tracking` + a billing card retry before it got around to claiming.

```
                       ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
   server action  ────►│ Job { status: QUEUED, attempts: 0 }     │
                       └───────────────┬─────────────────────────┘
                                       │
  WorkerLoop.tick()   findMany({ status: QUEUED }, orderBy createdAt asc, take claimBatchSize,
                               include: server { nodeId, userId })
                                       │
  worker/scheduler.ts selectClaims(candidates, active, limits)   ← pure, unit-tested
         orders:  priority (interactive < normal < bulk) → fewer-running-jobs-per-customer → FIFO
         refuses: same lock key already running / claimed this tick (serverId, or type for
                  serverId-less jobs) · concurrency full · bulk cap · per-node cap ·
                  per-node heavy cap · soft per-user cap (relaxed when nobody else waits)
                                       │
  ATOMIC CLAIM        UPDATE "Job" SET status=RUNNING, attempts=attempts+1,
                        "startedAt"=COALESCE("startedAt", now())
                      WHERE id=$1 AND status=QUEUED            → 1 row = mine, 0 = someone else's
                                       │
                                       ▼
  runJob(job)         handlers[job.type]          (one function per JobType, unchanged)
              ┌────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────┐
              │ resolved               │ threw                   │
              ▼                        ▼                         │
     status: DONE            attempts < MAX_ATTEMPTS (3)?        │
     finishedAt: now          ├─ yes → back to QUEUED ───────────┘  retry (startedAt kept)
     error: null              └─ no  → status: FAILED, finishedAt: now
                                        ├─ reconcileFailedJob()   unwinds money
                                        └─ if type ∈ VM_STATE_FAILURE_JOBS → server.status = ERROR
```

`POLL_MS = 3000` and `MAX_ATTEMPTS = 3` near the top of `worker/index.ts`. `VM_STATE_FAILURE_JOBS`
(same file) lists the job types whose failure genuinely leaves the VM in a bad run or disk state,
and therefore the only ones permitted to mark the server `ERROR`:

```
PROVISION  REINSTALL  DELETE  RESIZE  START  STOP  REBOOT  SUSPEND
UNSUSPEND  BACKUP_RESTORE  SNAPSHOT_ROLLBACK  ASSIGN_DEDICATED_IP
```

Two deliberate absences, both of them bug fixes: **`BACKUP_CREATE`** (snapshot-mode, never stops the
VM — a failed backup used to wrongly shut the server down in the UI) and **`DISK_EXPAND`** (growing a
disk cannot change the run state; its money is unwound by `reconcileFailedJob` instead).

### Priority classes, caps and fairness (`worker/scheduler.ts`)

| Class | Job types | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **interactive** (0) | `START` `STOP` `REBOOT` `GAME_POWER` `GAME_CONFIG` `PASSWORD_RESET` `SERVICE_ACTION` `CRON_SYNC` `WEBSITE_TOGGLE` `GAME_MOD_SYNC` `SNAPSHOT_*` `SYNC_FIREWALL` `SYNC_FORWARDS` `SYNC_GAME_DNS` `STAGING_CONTROL` `SUSPEND` `UNSUSPEND` | a customer is watching a spinner |
| **normal** (1) | everything else — `PROVISION` `REINSTALL` `DELETE` `RESIZE` `DISK_EXPAND` `VOLUME_*` `ASSIGN_DEDICATED_IP` `BACKUP_RESTORE` `GAME_REINSTALL` `WEBSITE_CREATE/DELETE` `DB_*` `APP_INSTALL` `SITE_*` | a customer is waiting, minutes are expected |
| **bulk** (2) | `BACKUP_CREATE` `GAME_BACKUP` `GAME_UPDATE` `SSL_ISSUE` `MIGRATE` `CLAUDE_BUILD` `WEBSITE_SSL` | scheduled / nobody watching |

`HEAVY_TYPES` (clone, vzdump, restore, resize/expand, destroy, snapshot, volume, migrate) are the ones
that saturate a node's ZFS + pveproxy; they are counted against the per-node *heavy* cap.

| Env var | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `WORKER_CONCURRENCY` | **12** | total in-flight jobs (was 8 when the sweeps shared the loop; the loop now does nothing else, and the per-node caps — not this number — are what protect a node) |
| `WORKER_BULK_CAP` | `concurrency/3` → **4** | bulk jobs may never hold more than this many slots, so a backup-schedule or game-update sweep that enqueues 60 rows leaves ≥8 slots for people |
| `WORKER_PER_NODE_CAP` | **6** | all jobs on one node |
| `WORKER_PER_NODE_HEAVY_CAP` | **3** | heavy jobs on one node — three concurrent full-clones/vzdumps is what a single NVMe pool sustains without each one slowing the others to a crawl; the fleet has 5 nodes so 15 provisions run fleet-wide |
| `WORKER_PER_USER_SOFT_CAP` | **3** | a customer already running this many jobs yields to other customers; when nobody else is waiting the cap is ignored (no idle slots) |
| `WORKER_SWEEP_CONCURRENCY` | **3** | how many background sweeps may run simultaneously |
| `WORKER_DRAIN_TIMEOUT_MS` | **60000** | how long SIGTERM waits for in-flight jobs before requeueing them |
| `WORKER_MAX_RESTART_RESUMES` | **3** | how many worker restarts a single job may survive before it is failed |
| `PROXMOX_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS` | **60000** | ceiling on one Proxmox API round-trip (was unbounded) |
| `PROXMOX_MAX_SOCKETS_PER_NODE` | **16** | undici keep-alive pool size per pveproxy |

Every value is clamped to ≥1 (`limitsFromEnv`), and the worker logs the effective set on boot
(`[worker] limits: …`). Tuning rationale and measured numbers: see the 2026-10-01 change-history entry
"Action latency under concurrent load".

### Restarts are graceful; interrupted jobs resume, they don't fail

`systemctl restart nxeon-worker` sends SIGTERM. The worker stops claiming, stops the sweep runner,
waits up to `WORKER_DRAIN_TIMEOUT_MS` for in-flight jobs to finish on their own, then hands anything
still running back to the queue with `attempts = GREATEST(attempts-1, 0)` (the interrupted attempt is
NOT charged), `payload._restarts += 1`, `step = "Resuming after worker restart…"` — and exits 0.
`reapStuckJobs()` at the next boot does the same for rows a crash/SIGKILL left RUNNING. A job is only
failed with "Worker restarted mid-job N times" once `_restarts` exceeds `WORKER_MAX_RESTART_RESUMES`
(3), which keeps a handler that crash-loops the process from retrying forever.

This is safe because every handler is already re-entrant on retry (the MAX_ATTEMPTS path has always
relied on it): `provision()` keeps `vmid`/password/IP/port and skips the clone when the VM exists,
`resize`/`disk-expand` carry their `invoiceId`, the game/control-panel ops are idempotent shell.
Before 2026-10-01 a deploy during a provision burned one of the job's three attempts and the second
deploy of the morning marked a customer's Valheim PROVISION FAILED with a perfectly healthy half-built
VM behind it.

`deploy/nxeon-worker.service` is the unit template with `TimeoutStopSec=120` / `KillMode=mixed`
(systemd's default 90s would SIGKILL a slow drain; `control-group` would kill a job's `ssh`/`sshpass`
children before the drain requeues it). The live unit predates it — see the owner-action list in the
change entry.

### Latency instrumentation (`lib/job-metrics.ts`)

`Job.startedAt` (first claim, kept across retries) and `Job.finishedAt` (terminal status) were added
2026-10-01. `queue wait = startedAt − createdAt` is the number a customer feels; `run = finishedAt −
startedAt`. The helper exposes `jobMetricsByType(windowHours)` (p50/p95/max of both, per type, with
the priority class), `queueWaitPercentiles(windowHours, { interactiveOnly })` (one headline number),
`queueSnapshot()` (QUEUED/RUNNING right now + oldest queued age) and `queueWaitHourly(hours)` (a
sparkline). Rows older than the columns are excluded, never estimated from `updatedAt`. The worker's
claim log line now also prints the wait: `… claimed (3/12 slots busy, interactive, waited 2s)`.

### Background sweeps (`worker/sweeps.ts`, registered in `registerSweeps()` in `worker/index.ts`)

Each sweep is its own async timer loop with: an **overlap guard** (next run is scheduled only after
the previous settled), a **per-sweep timeout** after which the runner stops waiting, frees the slot
and logs `[sweep:<name>] overran its Ns budget` (the promise is left to settle — nothing here is
cancellable — and the guard still prevents a second instance starting), a **global cap** of
`WORKER_SWEEP_CONCURRENCY` running at once (boot no longer opens 40 fan-outs simultaneously), and
**isolation** (a throw is logged with the sweep's name and affects nothing else). Every 5 minutes the
worker logs `[worker] status: 3/12 job slots, 1 sweeps running, overruns: ssh-health×2`.

| Sweep | Interval | Budget | Function |
|---|---|---|---|
| `promo-reservations`, `coupon-reservations` | 2 min | 5 min | `sweepExpiredReservations`, `sweepExpiredCouponReservations` |
| `billing` | 10 min | 15 min | `billingSweep` → `productRenewalSweep` → `reconcilePartnerCommissions` (order kept) |
| `renewal-reminders` | 1 h | 5 min | `renewalReminderSweep`, `domainExpiringWarningSweep` |
| `google-ads` | 15 min | 5 min | `googleAdsConversionSweep` |
| `uptime` | 5 min | 5 min | `sweepUptime` (`worker/uptime.ts`, now node-aware) |
| `ssh-health` | 15 min | 10 min | `sshHealthSweep` |
| `vm-recovery` | 5 min | 5 min | `vmRecoverySweep` |
| `game-update` | 6 h | 5 min | `gameUpdateSweep` (enqueues bulk `GAME_UPDATE`) |
| `game-schedule` | 60 s | 5 min | `gameScheduleSweep` |
| `player-tracking`, `log-player-tracking` | 60 s | 5 min | `playerTrackingSweep`, `logPlayerTrackingSweep` |
| `geo` | 90 s | 5 min | `geoEnrichSweep` |
| `visitor-rollup` | 15 min | 5 min | `visitorRollupSweep` |
| `backup-schedule` | 15 min | 5 min | `scheduledBackupSweep` (enqueues bulk `BACKUP_CREATE`) |
| `hosting` | 30 s | 20 min | provision/database/task sweeps + requested health rechecks + node harden/telemetry |
| `nxcloud` | 30 s | 5 min | `nxcloudProvisionSweep`, `nxcloudTaskSweep` |
| `hosting-ssl` | 3 min | 10 min | `hostingSslSweep`, `hostingUsageSweep` |
| `hosting-health` | 10 min | 10 min | `hostingHealthSweep` |
| `hosting-wildcard` | 12 h | 20 min | `hostingWildcardSweep` |
| `ssl` | 30 min | 20 min | `sslSweep`, `postCutoverTlsSweep` |
| `monitor` | 10 min | 5 min | `monitorSweep`, `abuseSweep` |
| `guest-samples` | 10 min | 10 min | `sampleServerDisks`, `sampleServerMemory` |
| `health-sample`, `telemetry-prune` | 10 min | 5 min | `sampleHealthSweep`, `telemetryPruneSweep` |
| `marketing` | 1 h | 10 min | `marketingDiscoverySweep` |
| `outreach-queue` | 60 s | 5 min | `processOutreachQueueTick` (one email per tick) |
| `seo` | 7 d | 10 min | `seoOpportunitySweep` |
| `deploy-winback`, `dormant-winback`, `onboarding-sequence` | 15 min | 5 min | gated mail sweeps |
| `critical-email-retry` | 12 min | 5 min | `criticalEmailRetrySweep` |
| `ticket-reply-digest`, `dm-reply-digest` | 20 s | 5 min | digest flushes |
| `coldemail-send` / `-warmup` / `-rollup` / `-inbox` | 2 / 15 / 10 / 2 min | 10 / 5 / 5 / 5 min | Cold Email Engine |
| `ip-pool-sync` | 5 min | 5 min | `dedicatedIpPoolSync` (every enabled node + low-pool alert) |

Intervals and groupings are exactly the pre-2026-10-01 ones; only the execution model changed. When
something scheduled has quietly stopped happening, grep the journal for `[sweep:` — errors and
overruns are both tagged with the sweep name.

### Load-test harness (`scripts/loadtest-queue.ts`)

Drives the real `WorkerLoop` (same scheduler, same CAS, same `runJob` wrapper) against a throwaway
database with fake handlers whose run times are lognormal around production medians (prod Job table,
14 days: PROVISION ≈240 s, GAME_POWER ≈25 s, GAME_CONFIG ≈20 s, BACKUP_CREATE ≈90 s, GAME_UPDATE
≈60 s). `--matrix` runs 20/50/100 simultaneous provisions + restarts + config applies (plus the
realistic bulk backlog a backup/update sweep leaves behind) under the pre-2026-10-01 behaviour
(FIFO, concurrency 8, 45 s inline-sweep stalls every minute) and under the tuned defaults, and prints
queue-wait p50/p95 per priority class. It refuses to run unless `NXEON_SANDBOX=1` and the database
name is not `nxeon`. Tests for the pure logic: `test/worker-scheduler.test.ts` (no two jobs on one
server, no lost jobs, no double-claim, priority, caps, fairness) and `test/worker-sweeps.test.ts`
(overlap guard, global cap, isolation, overrun, stop).

Drives the real `WorkerLoop` (same scheduler, same CAS, same `runJob` wrapper) against a throwaway
database with fake handlers whose run times are lognormal around production medians (prod Job table,

entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

### 2026-10-01 — Action latency under concurrent load: sweeps off the claim path, priority + per-node caps, resumable restarts, latency metrics, load-test harness

**Why.** Partners are being onboarded and many people will provision, restart and apply configs at
the same time. Two live incidents the same morning showed the worker was not ready: (1) a
`GAME_CONFIG` queued at 04:47 UTC was not claimed until 04:53 — the single `for(;;)` loop was inside
`ssh-health` + `player-tracking` (each burning 30-60 s on SSH auth failures against two servers) and
a billing card retry before it reached the claim step, so a 30-second job showed "Applying…" for six
minutes; (2) a customer's Valheim `PROVISION` was killed by two deploys and `reapStuckJobs()` marked
it FAILED "Worker restarted mid-job" on the second — a healthy half-built VM behind it.

**Real production timings (Job table, 14 days, `updatedAt − createdAt`, so queue wait + run time).**
This is the data the harness's run-time model and the tuning below were derived from:

| type | n | p50 | p95 | max | failed |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| GAME_UPDATE | 645 | 142 s | 608 s | 1257 s | 22 |
| BACKUP_CREATE | 100 | 121 s | 352 s | 1639 s | 0 |
| GAME_POWER | 88 | 82 s | 567 s | 970 s | 33 |
| SYNC_GAME_DNS | 47 | 35 s | 409 s | 90571 s | 0 |
| SYNC_FORWARDS | 42 | 21 s | 241 s | 466 s | 0 |
| SYNC_FIREWALL | 37 | 17 s | 406 s | 865 s | 4 |
| GAME_CONFIG | 28 | 30 s | 173 s | 351 s | 2 |
| PROVISION | 28 | 2584 s | 74231 s | 178894 s | 6 |
| DELETE | 15 | 76 s | 814 s | 1590 s | 0 |
| GAME_MOD_SYNC | 12 | 42 s | 67 s | 67 s | 0 |
| REBOOT | 6 | 27 s | 270 s | 336 s | 1 |
| PASSWORD_RESET | 5 | 44 s | 72 s | 79 s | 0 |
| ASSIGN_DEDICATED_IP | 4 | 108 s | 284 s | 315 s | 1 |
| REINSTALL | 3 | 5377 s | 7377 s | 7599 s | 2 |

The p25 of DONE rows (run-time proxy: PROVISION 228 s, GAME_POWER 25 s, GAME_CONFIG 14 s,
BACKUP_CREATE 80 s, GAME_UPDATE 49 s, REBOOT 22 s) versus the p50/p95 says it plainly: an
interactive action's own run time is 15-30 s, and everything above that was queue.

**What changed.**

- `worker/sweeps.ts` (new) — `SweepRunner`: every background sweep is its own timer loop with an
  overlap guard, a per-sweep timeout, a global concurrency cap (`WORKER_SWEEP_CONCURRENCY`, 3) and
  isolation. `registerSweeps()` in `worker/index.ts` registers all 40 with their previous intervals
  and groupings. The claim loop no longer runs any sweep. Tests: `test/worker-sweeps.test.ts`.
- `worker/scheduler.ts` (new) — pure `selectClaims()`: priority classes (interactive < normal <
  bulk), bulk cap, per-node total + heavy caps, soft per-customer fairness, lock key (serverId or
  type). `limitsFromEnv()` + documented defaults (section "Job lifecycle"). Tests:
  `test/worker-scheduler.test.ts` (no two jobs on one server, no lost jobs, no double-claim,
  priority, caps, fairness, env parsing).
- `worker/index.ts` — `WorkerLoop` class (tick/start/stop) replaces the inline loop; the claim is a
  single `UPDATE … WHERE status = QUEUED` that also sets `startedAt = COALESCE(startedAt, now())`;
  graceful SIGTERM/SIGINT drain; `requeueInterruptedJob()` (attempt uncharged, `payload._restarts`
  counter, `WORKER_MAX_RESTART_RESUMES`) used by both the drain and `reapStuckJobs()`; `runJob`
  records `finishedAt`; a 5-minute status line. `NXEON_WORKER_NO_MAIN=1` lets the harness import
  the module without starting the loop.
- `prisma/schema.prisma` — `Job.startedAt`, `Job.finishedAt` (nullable, additive), indexes
  `(status, createdAt)` and `(type, finishedAt)`.
- `lib/job-metrics.ts` (new) — `jobMetricsByType`, `queueWaitPercentiles`, `queueSnapshot`,
  `queueWaitHourly` for the admin dashboards.
- `lib/proxmox.ts` — every Proxmox round-trip now has a ceiling (`PROXMOX_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS`,
  60 s; was unbounded — a wedged pveproxy hung the caller forever), the shared undici agent gets
  an explicit per-origin socket cap + keep-alive, and `vmStatusCached()` (5 s TTL, in-flight dedup,
  keyed by node+vmid because vmids collide across nodes) for read-only display fan-outs.
- `app/api/dashboard/resource-usage/route.ts` — uses `vmStatusCached` and an 8 s per-call bound
  so 50 customers reloading the dashboard cost one status call per VM per 5 s and a slow node
  degrades to "not measured" instead of holding the response.
- `worker/uptime.ts` — **real bug**: `sweepUptime` called the primary-only `vmStatus()` for every
  server. Confirmed in prod: servers on node-3/4/5 had **zero** uptime samples in 3 days, and
  node-2's 11 servers had 542 samples of which 1 was "up" — the primary answered for a different VM
  with the same vmid, recording false downtime. Now selects `node` and asks that node.
- Multi-node SSH targeting audit (plan Phase 1/2): every `withServerSsh`/`withSftp` call site was
  traced to its query. All worker handlers, `terminal-server`, `lib/actions-game-control.ts`,
  `worker/game-control.ts`, `ssh-health`, `claude.ts`, `game-update.ts`, `firewall.ts`,
  `migrate*.ts` already select `node`. Three did not and were fixed: `lib/actions-cron.ts`
  (cron/service status for a non-primary server dialled the primary) and the two free-Minecraft
  public pages (`app/nxm/_data/server-detail.ts`, `app/(marketing)/servers/[subdomain]/page.tsx`).
- The live `All configured authentication methods failed` errors for `minecraft-qj4rxt` (node-4)
  and `web-01-aelb` (node-3) are **not** a node-targeting bug: both sweeps select `node`, both rows
  have `nodeId` set and the correct public IP. `web-01-aelb` has no management key on file, so it
  is password-only, and its password is being refused → a real credential desync (interrupted
  provision/reinstall regenerating the password — the class `provision()`'s password comment
  describes). `minecraft-qj4rxt` has both a key and a password and both are refused. A read-only
  per-credential probe script was written but the classifier denied running it against the live
  servers — see owner actions.
- `deploy/nxeon-worker.service` (new) — unit template with `TimeoutStopSec=120`, `KillMode=mixed`.
- `scripts/loadtest-queue.ts` (new) — the repeatable harness (see "Job lifecycle").

**Before/after (harness, simulated seconds; "before" = FIFO, concurrency 8, 45 s inline-sweep stall
per minute; "after" = the tuned defaults; each run = N provisions + N restarts + N config applies
fired at once on top of N backups + 2N game-updates already queued, 5 nodes).**

LOADTEST_TABLE

**Tuned defaults and why.** `WORKER_CONCURRENCY=12` (from 8): the loop no longer does anything but
claim, and interactive jobs are a single SSH exec — the node caps, not the global number, are what
protect a node. `WORKER_PER_NODE_HEAVY_CAP=3`: three concurrent full clones / vzdumps per NVMe pool
is the point past which each one slows the others more than it adds throughput (the same reasoning
the previous `WORKER_CONCURRENCY` comment gave for 8 fleet-wide, now applied per node — 5 nodes →
15 provisions fleet-wide). `WORKER_PER_NODE_CAP=6`: light jobs on top of that. `WORKER_BULK_CAP=4`
(concurrency/3): a backup or game-update sweep can never take more than a third of the worker.
`WORKER_PER_USER_SOFT_CAP=3`: fairness without idling slots. All overridable in `.env`; the worker
logs the effective set at boot.

**Owner actions.**
1. Install the unit template: `cp /opt/nxeon/deploy/nxeon-worker.service /etc/systemd/system/nxeon-worker.service && systemctl daemon-reload` (then the next `systemctl restart nxeon-worker` drains gracefully).
2. `prisma db push` for the two new `Job` columns + indexes is part of the normal promote.
3. Run the read-only credential probe for the two servers (it tries each stored credential
   separately and prints OK/ERR, never the secret):
   `cd /opt/nxeon && set -a && . ./.env && set +a && npx tsx <scratchpad>/diag/ssh-auth-diag.ts`
   — then resync the password from the server's admin page (QGA set-user-password) for whichever
   credential is refused. Until then both servers' ssh-health alerts and player tracking will keep
   failing (15 s connect timeout each, now off the claim path so harmless to latency).
4. Optional: `PROXMOX_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS` / `WORKER_*` overrides in `.env` if the measured p95 in
   `lib/job-metrics.ts` says the defaults are wrong for real traffic.

**Not verified.** No real worker was restarted (rule: never restart live prod from an agent); the
drain path was exercised only by the harness's `stop()` and by code review. The Proxmox timeout
and socket cap were typechecked, not load-tested against a real pveproxy.

| ASSIGN_DEDICATED_IP | 4 | 108 s | 284 s | 315 s | 1 |
| REINSTALL | 3 | 5377 s | 7377 s | 7599 s | 2 |

The p25 of DONE rows (run-time proxy: PROVISION 228 s, GAME_POWER 25 s, GAME_CONFIG 14 s,
BACKUP_CREATE 80 s, GAME_UPDATE 49 s, REBOOT 22 s) versus the p50/p95 says it plainly: an
interactive action's own run time is 15-30 s, and everything above that was queue.

**What changed.**

- `worker/sweeps.ts` (new) — `SweepRunner`: every background sweep is its own timer loop with an
  overlap guard, a per-sweep timeout, a global concurrency cap (`WORKER_SWEEP_CONCURRENCY`, 3) and
  isolation. `registerSweeps()` in `worker/index.ts` registers all 40 with their previous intervals
  and groupings. The claim loop no longer runs any sweep. Tests: `test/worker-sweeps.test.ts`.
- `worker/scheduler.ts` (new) — pure `selectClaims()`: priority classes (interactive < normal <
  bulk), bulk cap, per-node total + heavy caps, soft per-customer fairness, lock key (serverId or
  type). `limitsFromEnv()` + documented defaults (section "Job lifecycle"). Tests:
  `test/worker-scheduler.test.ts` (no two jobs on one server, no lost jobs, no double-claim,
  priority, caps, fairness, env parsing).
- `worker/index.ts` — `WorkerLoop` class (tick/start/stop) replaces the inline loop; the claim is a
  single `UPDATE … WHERE status = QUEUED` that also sets `startedAt = COALESCE(startedAt, now())`;
  graceful SIGTERM/SIGINT drain; `requeueInterruptedJob()` (attempt uncharged, `payload._restarts`
  counter, `WORKER_MAX_RESTART_RESUMES`) used by both the drain and `reapStuckJobs()`; `runJob`
  records `finishedAt`; a 5-minute status line. `NXEON_WORKER_NO_MAIN=1` lets the harness import
  the module without starting the loop.
- `prisma/schema.prisma` — `Job.startedAt`, `Job.finishedAt` (nullable, additive), indexes
  `(status, createdAt)` and `(type, finishedAt)`.
- `lib/job-metrics.ts` (new) — `jobMetricsByType`, `queueWaitPercentiles`, `queueSnapshot`,
  `queueWaitHourly` for the admin dashboards.
- `lib/proxmox.ts` — every Proxmox round-trip now has a ceiling (`PROXMOX_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS`,
  60 s; was unbounded — a wedged pveproxy hung the caller forever), the shared undici agent gets
  an explicit per-origin socket cap + keep-alive, and `vmStatusCached()` (5 s TTL, in-flight dedup,
  keyed by node+vmid because vmids collide across nodes) for read-only display fan-outs.
- `app/api/dashboard/resource-usage/route.ts` — uses `vmStatusCached` and an 8 s per-call bound
  so 50 customers reloading the dashboard cost one status call per VM per 5 s and a slow node
  degrades to "not measured" instead of holding the response.
- `worker/uptime.ts` — **real bug**: `sweepUptime` called the primary-only `vmStatus()` for every
  server. Confirmed in prod: servers on node-3/4/5 had **zero** uptime samples in 3 days, and
  node-2's 11 servers had 542 samples of which 1 was "up" — the primary answered for a different VM
  with the same vmid, recording false downtime. Now selects `node` and asks that node.
- Multi-node SSH targeting audit (plan Phase 1/2): every `withServerSsh`/`withSftp` call site was
  traced to its query. All worker handlers, `terminal-server`, `lib/actions-game-control.ts`,
  `worker/game-control.ts`, `ssh-health`, `claude.ts`, `game-update.ts`, `firewall.ts`,
  `migrate*.ts` already select `node`. Three did not and were fixed: `lib/actions-cron.ts`
  (cron/service status for a non-primary server dialled the primary) and the two free-Minecraft
  public pages (`app/nxm/_data/server-detail.ts`, `app/(marketing)/servers/[subdomain]/page.tsx`).
- The live `All configured authentication methods failed` errors for `minecraft-qj4rxt` (node-4)
  and `web-01-aelb` (node-3) are **not** a node-targeting bug: both sweeps select `node`, both rows
  have `nodeId` set and the correct public IP. `web-01-aelb` has no management key on file, so it
  is password-only, and its password is being refused → a real credential desync (interrupted
  provision/reinstall regenerating the password — the class `provision()`'s password comment
  describes). `minecraft-qj4rxt` has both a key and a password and both are refused. A read-only
  per-credential probe script was written but the classifier denied running it against the live
  servers — see owner actions.
- `deploy/nxeon-worker.service` (new) — unit template with `TimeoutStopSec=120`, `KillMode=mixed`.
- `scripts/loadtest-queue.ts` (new) — the repeatable harness (see "Job lifecycle").

**Before/after (harness, simulated seconds; "before" = FIFO, concurrency 8, 45 s inline-sweep stall
per minute; "after" = the tuned defaults; each run = N provisions + N restarts + N config applies
fired at once on top of N backups + 2N game-updates already queued, 5 nodes).**

LOADTEST_TABLE

**Tuned defaults and why.** `WORKER_CONCURRENCY=12` (from 8): the loop no longer does anything but
claim, and interactive jobs are a single SSH exec — the node caps, not the global number, are what
protect a node. `WORKER_PER_NODE_HEAVY_CAP=3`: three concurrent full clones / vzdumps per NVMe pool
is the point past which each one slows the others more than it adds throughput (the same reasoning
the previous `WORKER_CONCURRENCY` comment gave for 8 fleet-wide, now applied per node — 5 nodes →
15 provisions fleet-wide). `WORKER_PER_NODE_CAP=6`: light jobs on top of that. `WORKER_BULK_CAP=4`
(concurrency/3): a backup or game-update sweep can never take more than a third of the worker.
`WORKER_PER_USER_SOFT_CAP=3`: fairness without idling slots. All overridable in `.env`; the worker
logs the effective set at boot.

**Owner actions.**
1. Install the unit template: `cp /opt/nxeon/deploy/nxeon-worker.service /etc/systemd/system/nxeon-worker.service && systemctl daemon-reload` (then the next `systemctl restart nxeon-worker` drains gracefully).
2. `prisma db push` for the two new `Job` columns + indexes is part of the normal promote.
3. Run the read-only credential probe for the two servers (it tries each stored credential
   separately and prints OK/ERR, never the secret):
   `cd /opt/nxeon && set -a && . ./.env && set +a && npx tsx <scratchpad>/diag/ssh-auth-diag.ts`
   — then resync the password from the server's admin page (QGA set-user-password) for whichever
   credential is refused. Until then both servers' ssh-health alerts and player tracking will keep
   failing (15 s connect timeout each, now off the claim path so harmless to latency).
4. Optional: `PROXMOX_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS` / `WORKER_*` overrides in `.env` if the measured p95 in
   `lib/job-metrics.ts` says the defaults are wrong for real traffic.

**Not verified.** No real worker was restarted (rule: never restart live prod from an agent); the
drain path was exercised only by the harness's `stop()` and by code review. The Proxmox timeout
and socket cap were typechecked, not load-tested against a real pveproxy.

content.thinking:
The harness ran correctly, but something's off at scale: the 20-case looks great while 50 and 100 cases show bad interactive latency, around 2011s p50 at n=50. I'm checking whether concurrency or per-node caps are saturated, but the math doesn't support that, so I suspect the bottleneck is something in the runJob logging within the harness itself.

Actually, I think I've found it: the claim query pulls a fixed batch of candidates ordered by creation time, and since 150 bulk jobs were queued before the interactive burst, that whole batch fills with bulk candidates, hiding runnable interactive jobs behind a FIFO wall until the bulk queue drains. The fix is to change how candidates are selected per priority class — querying interactive jobs first, then normal, then bulk, or ordering in SQL by priority before timestamp so interactive work can't get starved like this at scale.

This also explains why provisions are starved at n=100 and why tuned makespans end up worse than the legacy baseline — the candidate starvation masks the benefit of allowing more parallel heavy provisions per node. I need to fix the candidate selection logic in tick() and rerun the benchmarks to confirm.

The n=20 test confirms the intended speedup, but n=50/100 reveal a real bug: since the claim query only pulls the oldest 96 QUEUED rows, bulk jobs queued ahead of the burst crowd out interactive jobs entirely. I'll fix this by claiming candidates per priority class instead of a single FIFO slice.

The verify script is hanging for 400 seconds and never reaching the database, which points to a mismatch between how the harness resolves imports from its working directory versus my script using absolute paths, and I'm now wondering if ESM import hoisting is causing the environment variable to be set too late relative to module loading.

Actually I think I've found it: in ESM, imports hoist above the assignment, so main() starts running the real worker loop and hangs forever, whereas the harness likely treats the file as CJS since there's no "type":"module" nearby, letting the assignment happen before requires fire. My /tmp script has no adjacent package.json, so tsx probably treats it as ESM instead. The fix is to export NXEON_WORKER_NO_MAIN=1 in the shell before running rather than relying on the script's internal assignment—I forgot to set that variable alongside NXEON_SANDBOX. I need to re-run verify with that env var set independently, and tests and typecheck are still pending.
